none: translation text only; no commentary points

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns three men who stayed behind and made no excuses before the Prophet's departure for Tabūk or after his return.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the three men who stayed behind, but offered no excuses, either before the Prophet left for Tabūk or after he returned.

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Some interpret being left behind as waiting for God's judgment, rather than being physically left behind from the Tabūk expedition.
rows.anchor: According to some, left behind here refers not to being left behind from the expedition to Tabūk, but to being left in a state waiting for God’s Judgment to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sources relate that Kaʿb ibn Mālik repeatedly delayed preparations through indecision and was left in Madinah with the other two when the army departed.
rows.anchor: Kaʿb ibn Mālik, who found himself in a perpetual state of indecision during the days leading up to the Tabūk campaign and kept putting off making the necessary preparations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kaʿb refused to invent an excuse, admitted he had none, and said he had never been better prepared for battle; he had joined many earlier battles with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: stated openly that he had no excuse, because at no time in his life was he materially more prepared to set out for battle than on the day the Prophet set out for Tabūk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet told Kaʿb and the other two to await God's decision, and the community was ordered to shun them.
rows.anchor: The Prophet told him and the other two to wait until God decided their case. Meanwhile, the community was commanded to shun them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During the fifty-day silence Kaʿb continued walking in the markets and praying in mosques, while the other two stayed home.
rows.anchor: although Kaʿb had the fortitude to walk in the markets and pray in the mosques while no one spoke to him, the other two remained in their homes for the fifty days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth closing in despite its breadth evokes constriction and loneliness, echoing the image in 9:25.
rows.anchor: That the earth, despite its breadth, closed in is also mentioned in v. 25; in the present verse it refers to the sense of constriction and loneliness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yūnus is the first of six sūrahs whose openings contain alif, lām, and rāʾ and speak of the Book.
rows.anchor: verses include the letters alif, lām, and rāʾ, and which speak of the Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is likely early Makkan, though 10:40 and 10:94–96 are said by JJ to be Madinan.
rows.anchor: With the possible exception of vv. 40, 94–96, which are said to have been revealed in Madinah (JJ), this sūrah in all likelihood belongs to the early Makkan period

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some date the sūrah to after the Prophet’s Night Journey and Ascension.
rows.anchor: Some say it is to be dated sometime after

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A central argument answers the Makkan charge that the Quran is fabricated: it is divine in origin and the Prophet did not compose it; the real fabricators reject God and face reckoning.
rows.anchor: One of this sūrah’s main arguments, in response to the Makkan idolaters’ accusations, is that the Quran is of Divine Origin and the Prophet had no hand in composing it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affliction makes even disbelievers manifest their true belief in God when no one else can help; once safe, they forget God and return to their old ways.
rows.anchor: even disbelievers manifest this true belief in God when affliction befalls them and they are left with no one to turn to except God; however, when they are safe, they forget God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah answers the Makkans’ challenge that the Prophet should hasten God's punishment if his claim is true.
rows.anchor: the challenges made by the Makkan idolaters that the Prophet should hasten to bring upon them the Punishment of God if he is truthful in his claims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also answers their demand for a different Quran that would not condemn their gods and would better suit their worship.
rows.anchor: that he should bring a different Quran that does not condemn their gods and is thus more congenial to their ways of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creatures ultimately return to God, just as their creation originated with Him.
rows.anchor: the ultimate return of all creatures is to God, just as their creation originated with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meeting God after death is inevitable; those devoted only to worldly life and false gods will be punished for disbelief.
rows.anchor: those who are given only to the life of this world and who serve their various false gods will be punished for their disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers receive glad tidings and are urged to remain patient through hardships inflicted by disbelievers.
rows.anchor: glad tidings (v. 2) are promised to the believers (see also vv. 4, 62–64, 103), who are encouraged to be patient with the hardships through which the disbelievers put them (v. 109)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are enveloped in peace, and God calls people to the Abode of Peace.
rows.anchor: It is the believers who will be engulfed in peace (v. 10), which is confirmed in God’s calling people to the Abode of Peace (v. 25).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah condemns conjecture, including belief in false gods and imagined intercession; intercession occurs only by God's leave.
rows.anchor: Another key theme is the futility of conjecture (vv. 36, 60, 66).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: False gods will disown their worshippers and cannot create or guide; God alone provides for creatures.
rows.anchor: the false gods will reject those who used to serve them (vv.28–29), especially because these false gods have no ability to create or guide others (vv. 34–35). Rather, God is the only One Who can provide for His creatures (v. 31).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers oppose truth from the outset and refuse to listen, explaining why people respond differently to guidance.
rows.anchor: disbelievers are opposed to the truth from the beginning and thus are not willing to listen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh eventually acknowledges the truth, but too late.
rows.anchor: there are people, like Pharaoh in v. 90, who will eventually acknowledge the truth, but too late.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance ultimately depends on God, and no one can guide those who are misguided.
rows.anchor: Ultimately, guidance is dependent upon God, and none can guide those who are misguided (vv. 42–43, 99, 100).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing accounts of Noah and Moses contrast with Jonah's people, who heed their prophet's warning and avert punishment, showing people can still accept truth and benefit by escaping punishment.
rows.anchor: Unlike the communities of Noah, Moses, and other previous prophets, the people of the prophet Jonah (from mention of whom in v. 98 the sūrah receives its name) heeded the warning of their prophet and thereby averted punishment.
